rv.q: Under the bright lights of 45th Street, though, the greatest foe of the musical “Almost Famous” is most definitely the film “Almost Famous.”
For anyone who spent their youth obsessing over great music and believing rock stars were, well, rock stars, Almost Famous will carry a dulcet pang of recognition.
It’s all entertaining enough — and no doubt a particular draw for the nostalgic baby-boomer-plus crowd — but there’s nothing extraordinary in the transformation to the stage.

But “Almost Famous” the musical, which features a perfectly likable book and cowritten lyrics by Crowe himself, is, dramaturgically speaking, not unlike “Mary Poppins,” with lumbering, big-haired musicians substituting for a British nanny.
It so desperately wants to remind you of something else you might’ve loved that the presiding emotional affect ends up being melancholy.
There’s no mud and guts to be found here.
If it’s for fans of musical theater unfamiliar with the film, then … there’s not much to recommend.
Nevertheless much of the quirky delicacy and emotional richness that made the movie so funny and moving are swamped by the inevitable need to amplify the material to fill a Broadway house.
It’s a feeble attempt to set up conflict for a musical that, inherently, has none.
And the stage version is so less good.

That leaves dumb, and I’m sorry to say that despite the intelligence of the 2000 movie on which it’s based, and the track record of its creators, the stage musical misses every opportunity to be the sharp, smart entertainment it might have been.
“Almost Famous” almost always works better with such winking gestures than it does with sappier ones.

In the end, you find yourself wishing that a production about the rebellious world of rock & roll would let its hair down a bit more and take bigger risks instead of playing it safe at almost every turn.
Without a strong focus, the story falls slack and meanders.
Chopping storytelling and a mystifying score keep Almost Famous from reaching the heights of its source material, but it’s not an entire waste.
Almost Famous is a musical that tries very hard to capture the spirit of Cameron Crowe's beloved 2000 film, but despite some lovely moments and a few soaring songs, it never quite takes flight.
Crowe’s Penny Lane is in a play, a musical —and not an especially powerful one, at that.
Thus, for those of us who attend shows hoping to be ushered through challenging, uncharted situations, these reenactments can be a bit of a bore.

Unfortunately, Crowe, who directed the musical and wrote the book from his Academy Award winning screenplay did not rethink his source material sufficiently for Broadway, probably feeling the songs would carry the day.
As the stage show offers nothing the movie did not already do and the new score is not very memorable, they will most likely be disappointed.

“Success” failed in its transfer as a Broadway musical ultimately because, in addition to having a weak score and book, its director never found a theatrical equivalent for the movie’s hard-edge chiaroscuro gaze of Manhattan night life in the 1950s.

While the production (directed by Jeremy Herrin) is polished and marked by seamless scene transitions, it represents little more than an uninspired simulacrum of the film in which the magic and charm has gotten lost in translation.
You are dealing with a virulent strain of pud-pulling mediocrity here.
Almost Famous is yet another conscientious, inspiration-free film adaptation, dedicated to recreating the original's key moments without ever acquiring an identity of its own.

Almost Famous: The Musical may well be the most dispiriting example of this screen-to-stage trend: a creatively bankrupt illustration of exactly the kind of commercialism that these characters rail against.
The result, on stage, is wince-inducing—a leaping, sing-songy, wishy-washy, toothless, sanitized, and humorless version of what that era of rock ‘n’ roll was.
It is a production so dull, with poor direction, ugly sets, uninteresting music, and flat performances, that it really needn’t exist at all.
Like a good old friend, Almost Famous takes you on a trip and brings you home safely.
For once, an adaptation is able to bottle all of a film’s magic and remain lavishly faithful to its script, while still injecting heart and humor of its very own flavor.

cn.t: Critics find this rock musical adaptation of Cameron Crowe's beloved film disappointingly tame and generic, with lackluster songs that fail to capture the movie's spirit, though Casey Likes' lead performance earns praise.

sg.ra: Wikipedia confirms the Jacobs orchestra floor is raked and the house has a single balcony (not two), so Center Orchestra rows A-D get close detail without the second-balcony crush. Playbill's Outsiders guide names Orchestra C Row B Seat 112 the best seat in the house; SeatPlan and Headout both call rows A-D the premium pick for plays specifically. Row numbering 101-114 (center block) means 107/108 sit dead-center on the aisle.

Multiple guides single out Center Orchestra rows F-K as the Jacobs value play: same centered sightline as the A-D premium block, but priced well below because Row I is where the mezzanine overhang line starts (overhead, not yet cutting into the stage). The Jacobs' single-balcony design and raked orchestra floor keep these rows clear, and Wikipedia notes two columns at the rear-of-orchestra promenade supporting the balcony - those sit behind Row N/O, so F-N stay clear of the columns.

SeatPlan and Headout both say the mezzanine overhang 'cuts into the top of the stage' starting at Row O - this is the Jacobs' specific geometry (mezz front at Row I, stage-top cutoff at Row O). Wikipedia adds that the rear-orchestra promenade has two columns supporting the balcony, so patrons here also share space with structural posts. Wheelchair spaces are assigned to rows I, J, P, and R per Headout, confirming P/R are flat promenade rows.

sg.vl: Fine if you pick single-digit seats
sg.ra: Side orchestra uses odd 1-27 (Left) and even 2-28 (Right). SeatPlan notes sightline restrictions intensify at double-digit seats (far aisle) and in back rows. Playbill's Outsiders guide specifically flagged that the right-side front rows were 'a clearer view' than left, because the show's tire set piece on house-left obstructs Orchestra L front rows - this is show-dependent but illustrates the Jacobs' shallow thrust style where side props block near side-orch seats. An AVFMS Orchestra G17 reviewer wrote 'sometimes the boxes block your view of the jungle gym' - the side boxes eat into side-orch sightlines.

sg.vl: Sharp angle, sells as obstructed for a reason
sg.ra: The Jacobs has 2 box seats on each side (16 total per Wikipedia) elevated beside the orchestra. TripAdvisor's theatre rep confirmed obstructed-view seats cluster 'on the extreme sides of the front mezzanine and orchestra' - the boxes are the prime example. Multiple guides warn boxes 'cut off high center stage scenes' and block views of stage-left from the right box / stage-right from the left box. SeatPlan explicitly recommends left boxes over right because the right box loses more stage-left content.

sg.vl: Elevated wide view, 9 rows from stage
sg.ra: SeatPlan names Center Mezz rows A-B the best mezz view in the Jacobs; an AVFMS reviewer at Mezz A107 wrote 'you are perfectly centered and at only nine rows from the stage' - the Jacobs' single-balcony design (per Wikipedia, no second balcony) means the mezz sits close rather than stacked high. Row B dodges Row A's safety-bar issue that SeatPlan calls 'obstructive to shorter patrons.' Front mezz is 168 seats in rows A-D with premium centered sightlines on the full set.

sg.vl: Row E is the legroom hack
sg.ra: Rear mezz is 252 seats in rows E-K. The Jacobs-specific quirk: Row E sits directly behind the front-mezz cross-aisle with a curtain/bannister (not a wall), giving 'extra space' for taller patrons per SeatPlan - Playbill's Outsiders guide confirms Mezz Left Row E has 'a curtained divider between the aisle and row' for extra legroom. Rows G-K are flagged as value seats because the mezz has a 'good rake' and Wikipedia confirms the Jacobs has only one balcony so even Row K stays surprisingly close. An AVFMS Mezz H22 reviewer noted 'legroom is not great' - stick to Row E or aisle seats.
